# Timer Loop

A timer loop wakes on a schedule (a cron job, a CI scheduled workflow) and
does one bounded unit of work, rather than running continuously. Use this
for maintenance-shaped work with no single "done" state -- triage, sweeps,
periodic checks.

## Stop condition

- Each invocation stops after completing exactly one unit of work (one
  triage pass, one sweep), regardless of whether more work is queued -- the
  next scheduled run picks up where this one left off.
- One unit of work, for this repository's own CI-driven timer loop (the
  `self-assess` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`), is: run `verify --run`
  once, run `assess --min-level 4` once against the fresh result, and, on
  `main` only, refresh `harness-badge.json` if the level or score changed.
  It never retries within the same invocation on failure -- the next push
  or the next scheduled trigger is the retry.

## Budget cap

- Max iterations per invocation: 1 (one `verify --run` + one `assess` pass;
  never loops internally).
- Wall-clock cap per invocation: 10 minutes, matching `exec.mjs`'s own
  `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS` (300s) per declared command with headroom for three
  declared commands (bootstrap, test, lint) run back to back.
- Schedule: every push to `main` and every pull request (see the `on:`
  block in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`) -- event-triggered, not cron-based,
  since this project's timer loop exists to keep the badge honest at the
  moment the tree actually changes, not on an arbitrary clock.
- A run that hits its cap mid-task exits cleanly and leaves state (via
  `PROGRESS.md` or `feature_list.json`) for the next scheduled run to
  resume from, instead of leaving something half-done and unrecorded.
